title: The scholar of Konya
hook: he becomes a respected teacher of Islamic law and theology in Konya, Anatolia

segments.voice: Yesterday, Balkh, and a boy's long road west to Konya. Your line was the road west.

Some people grow up into their parent's job. The kid who took over the family store, the doctor whose mother was a doctor, the pastor's son who became the pastor. People nod at them in the street. They're solid. They're safe. Konya, the early 1240s. A man in his mid-thirties, in a scholar's robe and a large turban, walks to teach his classes with students trailing behind him. People bring him legal questions and wait for his answer. He is exactly what everyone expected. If his life had stopped here, he might be remembered only as a learned man of Konya.
screen: `BECOMING YOUR PARENT'S JOB.` → `A ROBE, A TURBAN, STUDENTS.` → `THE SCHOLAR OF KONYA.`

segments.voice: Konya in the 1200s was the capital of the Seljuk sultans of Rum, a Muslim kingdom in Anatolia, full of mosques, schools and caravans. The sources say the sultan invited Rumi's father to teach there. In 1231 the father died, and his post passed to his son, who was about twenty-four. That's young to inherit a pulpit, so the son kept studying. Burhan al-Din of Tirmidh, a former student of his father, came to Konya and, the accounts say, trained him for about nine years, in books and in the inner life of prayer and fasting. The young man also studied in Aleppo and Damascus, two old centers of learning. By the early 1240s he was a respected teacher of Islamic law and theology, what Muslims call fiqh and kalam. He taught in a school, preached in the mosque, gave legal opinions, and was addressed as Mowlana, our master. He had a wife and sons; the oldest, Sultan Walad, would one day write his father's story. Here's what's worth noticing. The sources show no sign yet of the poet. They describe a learned, careful, deeply religious man. The wildness came later, and it grew out of this ground, not against it. His poems are full of the Qur'an and of law and theology, because he'd spent his whole life inside them. The respectable one was not a mask he later threw off. It was the soil.
screen: `KONYA, CAPITAL OF THE SELJUKS.` · `HIS FATHER'S POST AT TWENTY-FOUR.` · `NINE YEARS WITH BURHAN AL-DIN.` · `A TEACHER OF LAW AND THEOLOGY.` · then, large: `THE RESPECTABLE ONE.`

segments.voice: If the people who know you described you in three words, what would they say? Reliable, funny, the one who fixes things, the one who's always busy. Say the words inside, then ask gently: is that all of me, or is there something in me nobody has met yet? Don't answer quickly; leave the question open.
Mowlana, our master: the title Rumi's students used for him as a teacher of Islamic law and theology. Today's word.
Your line: the respectable one. It can be true without being the whole story. Day one hundred fifty-nine, in the books.

howItsDone: Readers of Rumi often begin with his life as a scholar: he taught Islamic law and theology in Konya, and biographies stress that his later poetry grew out of that learning.

notes: Review 2026-10-01: hook no longer leans on 'most of us know' and 'now picture'; softened 'almost nobody would know his name' and 'the great centers of learning'; 'no sign of the poet' attributed to the sources; Quran spelled Qur'an to match the path.
Father's death in 1231 and Rumi's age (about 24) follow the standard chronology. Confirm.
Burhan al-Din Muhaqqiq Tirmidhi's training for about nine years (c. 1232–1240/41) and study in Aleppo and Damascus: confirm.
Sultan's invitation to Baha al-Din: the sources name Ala al-Din Kayqubad I; unnamed here. Confirm.
Rumi as teacher of fiqh (Hanafi) and kalam, preacher, giver of legal opinions: confirm the description.
Sultan Walad (b. 1226) as eldest son and author of the Ibtida-nama: confirm.
